data.title: Live updates: Senate faces day of big votes with Blanche's nomination on the ropes
data.description:
The Senate is scrambling to leave for its August recess but has several hurdles to jump before it gets there after a week of infighting.

The biggest items on the list include acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination for the permanent job. On Friday morning, Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) announced she was a “no” vote, leaving Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) little room to maneuver. If Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) also becomes a “no,” the nomination may need to be put on ice.

Starting with a morning vote series, the upper chamber will try to pass a Russia sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) and a bloc of nominees. It will also vote on college sports legislation and a continuing resolution to fund the government into December.

President Trump on Friday has policy meetings at the White House and a roundtable at the State Department, before heading to Bedminster, N.J.

Follow live here.

data.title: US loses 23k jobs in July, unemployment dips slightly
data.description:
The U.S. economy lost 23,000 jobs in July, and the unemployment rate dipped slightly to 4.1 percent, according to new data released Friday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). 

Economists had expected American employers to add 83,000 jobs and the jobless rate to hold steady at 4.2 percent last month, according to consensus estimates. 

This comes on the heels of relatively weak jobs numbers in June, in which the U.S. workforce initially saw just 57,000 new roles added, well below the 110,000 that experts anticipated.  

Both the May and June jobs reports, however, were revised lower Friday by a combined 103,000. The updated numbers now show employers adding just 20,000 jobs last month, while the prior month’s job gains were reduced from 129,000 to 63,000.

President Trump and Republican lawmakers are grappling with persistent inflation and a relatively sluggish economy just three months out from the midterm elections, in which affordability has become a central issue. 

Annual inflation dipped slightly to 3.7 percent in June, according to the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation.  

This was down from a three-year high of 4.1 percent in May, as a brief ceasefire with Iran eased energy prices on hopes that ships would begin transporting more oil through the Strait of Hormuz. 

It’s unclear whether inflation will continue to trend downward, after Washington and Tehran began trading strikes again in early July. However, hostilities eased in recent days, as Iran and Oman have negotiated over a potential deal to reopen the key waterway. 

Meanwhile, the economy showed signs of slowing in the second quarter, with U.S. gross domestic product (GDP) increasing at an annual rate of 1.5 percent, down from 2.1 percent in the prior three-month period. 

The Fed, which met in mid-July, opted to hold interest rates steady in a split 9-3 decision. It marked the fifth straight time the rate-setting panel has voted to keep rates at their current level, even as Trump has put pressure on new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh to cut rates. 

Following the meeting, Warsh touted the economy’s “impressive resilience” in the face of “recent shocks,” while maintaining that the central bank is “resolute” in bringing inflation down to the Fed’s target rate of 2 percent.

data.title: Crenshaw weighs in on 'dumb' $20 burrito sparking debate over affordability
data.description:
Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas) doubled down on his comments Thursday after drawing criticism for telling Americans concerned about high food prices to “stop whining” and “get a job,” as a viral debate over the cost of a $20 burrito exposed divisions among the GOP over affordability.

“Just hearing about this dumb $20 burrito debate so just thought I’d make the losers on social media angry before going to bed,” Crenshaw posted on social platform X late Wednesday.

“Stop whining, get a job, eat Ramen like the rest of us did in college, on a budget with 4 roommates,” he wrote. “The market doesn’t care what you think something ‘should’ cost.”

After taking some heat in his comment section, the lawmaker sent out another post to address the backlash before doubling down on his previous remarks.

“Okay, I am SORRY for triggering the comment section,” Crenshaw wrote on X. 

The Texas Republican then sarcastically suggested the existence of a $20 burrito was proof capitalism had failed before making it clear he was joking.

“Remember when the right had principles and made fun of leftists for elevating victimhood as a virtue? Want to tell people the truth? Or just bribe them for their vote in the next election?” he wrote.

Crenshaw, who recently lost his bid for reelection, had ironically criticized the Biden administration in 2021 after it told Americans to eat less take-out beef and poultry to mediate inflation.

“America: our food prices are too high what are you doing about inflation? Biden admin: just be vegan and stop complaining you bunch of rubes,” he said in his 2021 post.

The burrito debate began earlier this week, after Turning Point USA spokesperson Andrew Kolvet shared a conversation with a college student who summed up his concerns about affordability by saying, “A burrito shouldn’t cost $20.”

“A lot of this is a hangover from Covid and Biden-era inflation, but the lived experience is the same: It just feels like basic things cost too much,” Kolvet wrote online.

Vice President Vance also weighed in on the discussion, after Washington Post columnist and Fox News contributor Marc Thiessen dismissed Kolvet’s complaint.

“Cry me a river. The burritos in the college cafeteria are included in your meal plan,” Thiessen wrote.

Vance replied to Thiessen with a jab about his weight.

“I’m surprised to hear Mark say this,” Vance wrote on X. “If you’ve ever met him in person, it’s quite obvious the man has never missed a burrito.”

Kolvet later told NewsNation’s “On Balance” that he “had no idea” that his comments would spur such a debate, but that it would be a mistake for the GOP to repeat the mistakes of former President Biden by dismissing the concern about food prices.

“I think it’s political malfeasance to ignore and deny the actual anxieties of voters, especially young voters,” he said.

data.title: Section 31 tariffs are meant to be a scalpel, not a sledgehammer
data.description:
Congress never intended for Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act to be a general tariff statute. It wrote the statute as a targeted trade remedy. That distinction matters. In fact, it’s at the heart of the latest lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s Section 301 tariffs.  

The case, brought by the Liberty Justice Center, nominally concerns tariffs on imports from 60 economies for their alleged failures to combat forced labor. But the bigger question is whether Section 301 remains a targeted trade remedy, or whether it’s been transformed into a general source of presidential tariff authority?

The statute itself provides the answer. 

Section 301 establishes a clear statutory chain. The U.S. Trade Representative must identify a particular foreign “act, policy, or practice,” determine that it burdens or restricts U.S. commerce and explain why the chosen response is an “appropriate and feasible” means of securing the elimination of the practice. 

That sequence is not a procedural formality. It is the statute’s limiting principle. 

Congress designed Section 301 as targeted economic diplomacy. Tariffs are not the objective; they are the instrument. Their purpose is to induce a foreign government to abandon a particular practice.

The stronger the connection between the identified practice and the chosen remedy, the more faithfully the executive is carrying out Congress’s design. The latest litigation argues that the connection has broken down. 

No one disputes that forced labor is a grave human rights abuse. The question before the court of International Trade is whether nearly uniform tariffs imposed on substantially all imports from 60 economies are an “appropriate and feasible” means of persuading each of those governments to strengthen enforcement against forced labor. 

That is precisely the inquiry Congress required. If the executive no longer must demonstrate how a tariff is likely to eliminate the specific foreign practice it identifies, then Section 301 ceases to function as Congress intended. It becomes something much broader: authority to impose tariffs whenever the executive concludes that another country’s policies deserve economic pressure. 

That’s not what Congress enacted. The broader structure of American trade law confirms the point. 

Congress has never delegated tariff authority through a single all-purpose statute. Instead, it created specialized authorities for specialized problems. Section 232 addresses national security, for example, and Section 122 authorizes temporary, across the board tariffs during balance of payments crises. Section 301 occupies a very different role by authorizing targeted responses to specific foreign trade practices. 

The distinctions are deliberate. Congress wanted different legal standards to govern different exercises of presidential power. 

Section 122 illustrates why that matters. Congress anticipated that presidents might seek broad tariffs affecting virtually the entire economy. It granted that authority but imposed strict limits. Under this statute, tariffs can’t exceed 15 percent and can only remain in effect for a maximum of 150 days without congressional approval. 

Those restrictions reflect a legislative judgment that economy-wide tariff authority should be temporary and politically accountable. Yet, if Section 301 can be interpreted to sustain substantially similar tariff programs indefinitely, those limits lose their force. A statute Congress designed for targeted trade retaliation starts performing the work Congress assigned elsewhere under much tighter constraints. 

Courts ordinarily reject interpretations that produce that result. One of the oldest principles of statutory interpretation is that Congress does not legislate redundantly. Statutes should complement one another, not allow one delegation to swallow the rest. That principle should guide the Court of International Trade here.

This case is not ultimately about whether tariffs are good policy or whether forced labor deserves a forceful response. It’s about whether courts will preserve the statutory limits Congress placed on one of its most consequential delegations of economic authority. 

Congress did not delegate a general power to impose tariffs whenever the executive identifies an international problem worthy of economic pressure. It authorized a far narrower authority: identify a specific foreign act, policy or practice, determine that it burdens U.S. commerce and justify the chosen tariff as an appropriate and feasible means of eliminating that practice. 

That statutory chain is not a technicality. It is what distinguishes Section 301 from a general tariff law. 

If courts allow that chain to be broken, Section 301 will no longer be a targeted trade remedy. It will become the executive branch’s default source of tariff authority whenever other statutes prove unavailable or inconvenient. That would do more than expand Section 301. It would erase one of the principal limits that Congress placed on the executive’s authority to impose tariffs. 

Section 301 was written to be a scalpel. Courts should not allow it to become a sledgehammer. 

Marc L. Busch is the Karl F. Landegger Professor of International Business Diplomacy at the Walsh School of Foreign Service, Georgetown University. Petros Mavroidis is the Edwin B. Parker Professor of Foreign and Comparative Law at Columbia Law School.

data.title: Trump declines to back Thune for another term as Senate GOP leader
data.description:
President Trump declined to back Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-N.D.) for a second term as Republican leader in the chamber, saying he did not want to discuss the matter, in an interview that aired on Friday. 

“I don’t want to get into that necessarily,” Trump told Punchbowl News. 

“I get along with him. It’s unfortunate that he doesn’t have the votes,” he said, referring to Thune insisting Senate Republicans do not have the votes to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act. 

When pressed on whether he gets along with Thune, Trump said, “I do,” but noted he has disagreements with the Senate leader. 

“I believe strongly in terminating the filibuster, and by the way, getting SAVE America Act approved immediately, and about 400 other things in every hour of every day,” the president said. 

Thune has repeatedly said Senate Republicans do not have the votes to pass the SAVE America Act and has thrown cold water on the prospect of eliminating the filibuster. The topic has become a point of contention between them. 

Trump warned that Democrats would move to eliminate the filibuster if they take back control of the chamber because they would be able to pass legislation with a simple majority. 

“If they get in, they’re going to do it very quickly,” the president said. “I would do whether they did it or not. We would get in the next two and a half years, we would get things that nobody ever dreamt of. We would be in office for the next hundred years.” 

“And I tell you what, if they get it in, I will be the last Republican president,” he said.

data.title: Trump says he would 'probably' get along with Jeffries as Speaker
data.description:
President Trump predicted in an interview aired early Friday he would “probably” get along with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) if Democrats take back the majority in the lower chamber in the midterm elections.

“I’d probably get along with him very well,” Trump told Punchbowl News when asked if he could do business with Jeffries. 

Trump called Jeffries “a nice guy,” recalling his meeting with the Democratic leader at the White House in 2025. 

“I think he’s a nice guy,” the president said. “He was here. We had a good meeting.” 

When pressed on Jeffries’s past criticisms and attacks on him, Trump said the New York Democrat is “harsh because I’m harsh on him.”

Trump and Jeffries have exchanged numerous verbal blows in the past, with Trump blasting Jeffries as “a low I.Q. individual” and urging Republicans to remove him from office. Jeffries, in turn, has said Trump has “Jeffries derangement syndrome,” which is a play on “Trump derangement syndrome.”

A Jeffries speakership is becoming a very real possibility ahead of the midterms, and one Trump would have to grapple with as he seeks to push his agenda through Congress. 

The president’s comments come as Democrats lead Republicans on the generic ballot ahead of November’s midterm elections. 

A CNN poll released last week showed Democrats leading Republicans on the generic ballot by 8 points. The Decision Desk HQ polling average currently has Democrats leading Republicans by just over 6 points.

data.title: Republicans can't just commie-punch their way to victory
data.description:
Republicans need to make some noise. It’s not enough to gloat over the rise of what many in the Republican Party consider the loony left. Rather, Republicans must convince voters they deserve to keep the majority in the House and the Senate. And currently, their message is thin.

Republicans are practically salivating over the nomination of Abdul El-Sayed, an anti-Israel Muslim extremist, to run for the seat held by the retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.). El-Sayed’s victory improves their chances hopes of flipping the blue seat red in November. Former House Intelligence Chairman Mike Rogers (R), a well-respected businessman, will face off against El-Sayed; in head-to-head polling, the Republican just barely leads.

But the Socialists convulsing the Democratic Party are not only chalking up wins in deep blue territories. They are also making inroads in a country which, having taken too much for granted, has grown less enthusiastic about capitalism and less supportive of our long-time ally Israel.

Republicans have taken to calling opponents “communists,” aware that the “socialist” label no longer destroys a candidate’s chances. And that is especially true among young people; according to polling by the CATO Institute, nearly two-thirds of Americans ages 18 to 29 have a favorable view of socialism. That is who voted for El-Sayed. Polling indicates that some 80 percent of young people favored the Leftist former health official over the establishment-backed Haley Stevens. El-Sayed ran especially well in college towns; surveys show that it is mainly white liberals with college and graduate degrees who are hearing the siren call of the socialist left.

Democrats’ advantage in the generic ballot, now at 7 points according to the Real Clear Polling averages, is slightly lower than it was a few months ago, which might indicate a repudiation of the slide towards collectivism. But other surveys, like those from CNN and Marquette, show voters viewing Democrats more favorably than they did last spring. It may be the leftward thrust of the party is actually helping the party’s standing.

For Republicans, that should be alarming. Nate Silver has suggested that Republicans could keep the House (which he calls a “low-probability event”) if the economy is booming (which it is) and if Republicans win “the argument that Democrats are too far left.”

For sure, Republicans need to talk up the extreme and anti-American ideas being touted by some on the Left — dangerous ideas like abolishing the police and prisons, and eliminating the Electoral College and the U.S. Senate. In 2021, at the peak of the Woke Era, state Rep. Francesca Hong, frontrunner for the Democratic nomination to be Wisconsin’s next governor, called for cancellation of Thanksgiving as a culturally insensitive celebration.

But it’s not enough just to point out all of the kookery. Republicans must also show voters how they will make their lives better. Just as it was not enough for Democrats to make hating President Trump the central plank of their party’s platform for the last decade, Republicans cannot rely solely on the public’s aversion to antisemitism and anti-Americanism to win elections. They must offer something positive — something better.

With only 90 days left before the midterm elections, time is running out to do that. The frustration for many of us is that our elected officials do not even seem to be trying.

Republicans control both houses of Congress but have barely taken advantage of that majority in the last year. While the first year of Trump’s second term saw the passage of the Big Beautiful Bill, which saved average American families thousands of dollars in taxes, the last several months have yielded few wins.

Congress did pass a roughly $70 billion reconciliation bill that funded ICE and Customs and Border Patrol through the balance of Trump’s term. But that is hardly the stuff of campaign messaging. Trump’s success in closing the border has caused the issue to recede among voters’ priorities.

The SAVE Act, a popular bill promising to make our elections more secure, has been mired, with several Republican senators blocking its inclusion in reconciliation bills. Most Americans — Republican and Democrat — approve of voter ID laws, but the bill includes other features like limits on mail-in ballots and proof of citizenship that some found troublesome. Instead of coalescing around a one-issue bill requiring voter ID, and forcing Democrats to vote against it, Republicans sent Congress home.

Meanwhile, efforts to create a third reconciliation package and advance other Republican priorities have come to naught. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) appears unwilling or unable to push further tax cuts, even though polling indicates such measures would be popular.

Recent surveys conducted by right-leaning pollster John McLaughlin show a majority of voters (51 percent) “want Congress to enact additional tax cuts to accelerate economic growth,” whereas only 26 percent “believe the recent tax reductions are sufficient.” He also found that 71 percent would back a measure allowing homeowners to transfer their low-interest mortgages to new homes, which would instantly increase housing inventory. Two-thirds of respondents favored “reducing income tax rates to 12 percent for middle-income Americans currently paying 22 percent or 24 percent.”

Another strong majority wants to index capital gains taxes for inflation, so that those who sell houses or stocks are not forced to pay taxes on phantom gains.

McLaughlin concludes that nearly 60 percent of voters would like to see a reconciliation package that “combines middle-class tax relief, reductions in waste and fraud, proof of citizenship and voter identification requirements, and other pro-growth reforms.”

There is the playbook; Republicans should jump on it and Trump should push for it, too.

Additionally, they must advertise not only the gains in the One Big Beautiful Bill, but talk up our capitalist system, emphasizing the opportunities that abound in our economy and under this administration. It is no surprise that entrepreneurship has never been hotter, with a huge surge the number of new companies being created.

McLaughlin found that voters repudiate Socialism when it is connected to Big Government solutions. Similarly, they embrace capitalism when it is tied to free markets.

Republicans need to connect those dots.

Liz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.

data.title: Murkowski will oppose Blanche nomination, putting it in danger of stalling
data.description:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) on Friday became the second Republican senator to announce she will vote against acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination to serve in the role full-time, putting his confirmation on a knife’s edge as one more “no” vote could sink or delay it.

Murkowski said she had “numerous constructive meetings with Blanche” and expressed appreciation for the trip he took to Alaska last month to learn about the law-enforcement challenges faced by remote communities. Still, the Republican questioned whether he would serve as an effective check on President Trump while leading the Justice Department (DOJ).

“The politicization — even weaponization — of the Department did not start with this administration but has accelerated during it. I take issue with the handling of the release of the [Jeffrey] Epstein files; the sweeping immunity protections granted to the President, his family, and their businesses; the statements that have been made to anti-abortion groups; and the repeated targeting of individuals ranging from former administration staff to sitting U.S. Senators,” Murkowski said.

The senator also raised concerns about whether Blanche would continue to oppose the establishment of a nearly $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund to compensate MAGA allies once he is confirmed.

“I am also keenly aware that the Department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund — which likely would have rewarded January 6 protesters — is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage,” she said. “Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds.”

Murkowski argued that the nation needs a chief law enforcement officer to “check the worst impulses of this administration” and questioned whether Blanche would do that.

“I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case,” the Alaska Republican added.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who faces a tough reelection race in November, announced earlier this week that she would vote against Blanche.

Collins called the acting attorney general “a capable lawyer” but warned that the DOJ under his leadership has “become increasingly political.”

She added that Blanche’s actions during his tenure as deputy attorney general “further eroded the department’s independence” and cited that as “the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation.”

The Maine senator also noted that he approved the order to shield Trump, his sons and the Trump Organization from IRS audits, sweeping immunity “unavailable to other American taxpayers,” and cited his role in approving the $1.776 billion “anti-weaponization” fund.

Collins then raised issues with Blanche’s pledge to an anti-abortion organization that he would seek to prohibit the mailing of abortion medication to women nationwide.

And she criticized federal prosecutors’ efforts under his leadership to indict Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) over a video they produced urging U.S. service members to resist unlawful orders.

Murkowski’s and Collin’s opposition to Blanche’s nomination means that Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) can afford only one more GOP defection and still confirm Blanche. Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) remains absent from the Senate after suffering a fall last month.

While McConnell is away, Thune has an effective majority of 52 seats and all 47 members of the Senate Democratic caucus are expected to oppose Blanche.

The one remaining undecided Republican is Sen. Bill Cassidy (La.), who has clashed with Trump over several high-profile issues recently, including the proposed compensation fund and congressional oversight of the war with Iran.

Cassidy met with his staff on Thursday to discuss Blanche’s nomination and he met with him earlier in the week in the basement of the Capitol. So far, however, the senator has declined to comment on how he might vote.

The Senate is expected to vote Friday or sometime over the weekend on a procedural motion to advance Blanche to a final confirmation vote.

data.title: Trump says GOP voters 'angry' at congressional Republicans ahead of midterms but not at him
data.description:
President Trump in an interview aired early Friday appeared to deflect blame for the anger among the Republican base toward the party’s leadership in Congress, saying in an interview published early Friday GOP voters are not “angry” with his job as president. 

“They’re angry at Republicans but they’re not angry at me,” Trump told Punchbowl News. 

Trump said the question for Republicans ahead of the midterms is if the party’s base will turn out to vote in November when he is not at the top of the ballot. 

“That’s the one thing I can’t tell [you]. I’m going to ask them to,” the president continued. 

“The question is will they vote because a lot of them are very angry at Republicans,” he said. 

A slew of recent polls show Trump with low approval ratings, which could threaten Republicans running in midterm races. 

A Quinnipiac University poll released last week found that only 32 percent of all registered voters said they support how Trump has handled his second term in office.

A separate CNN survey released last week showed Democrats leading Republicans on the generic ballot by 8 points. The Decision Desk HQ polling average currently has Democrats leading Republicans by just over 6 points. 

While Trump has recently clashed with some Republicans on Capitol Hill, particularly in the Senate, the president has recently hit the campaign trail to bolster GOP enthusiasm ahead of the midterms. 

Trump rallied supporters at an event highlighting the “No Taxes on Tips” provision of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in Las Vegas on Wednesday. 

Updated at 7:40 a.m. EDT

data.title: Our current housing crisis began in 2008 — and it never ended
data.description:
America’s housing crisis has been rightly blamed on a lack of supply. Lately the finger has been pointed at inflation as the driving force behind it.

Some evidence seems to support that notion. Home prices remain stubbornly high. Mortgage rates have more than doubled from their pandemic lows. Insurance premiums are soaring. Construction costs continue to rise, and rents consume an ever-larger share of household budgets.

But inflation did not create America’s housing crisis. It only exposed it.

To understand why millions of Americans are struggling to find housing they can afford, we need to look beyond the economic headlines of the last few years and revisit a crisis that began nearly two decades ago, in the wreckage of the Global Financial Crisis.

When the housing market collapsed in 2008, the damage extended far beyond foreclosures and failing banks. Homebuilders went out of business. Construction workers left the industry. Lending tightened dramatically. Investment dried up. Housing production fell off a cliff.

The economy eventually recovered, but housing production never did. In fact, the 2010s saw the fewest single-family home construction starts since at least the 1960s and nearly half as many as the decade that preceded it.

Now, Freddie Mac estimates the nation is short by about 3.7 million homes of what is needed to meet demand. The National Low Income Housing Coalition estimates that there is a shortage of 7.2 million rental homes affordable to renters with incomes at or below the federal poverty guideline.

A recent report from my organization’s National Housing Strategic Initiatives team notes that housing production dropped considerably in the aftermath of the financial crisis and “has failed to catch up with current demand.” The report argues that the effects of the housing crash continue to echo throughout today’s market, helping to drive the affordability challenges confronting households across the country.

That observation should fundamentally change how we think about housing affordability.

While the conventional narrative treats today’s crisis as a recent phenomenon driven by inflation, interest rates, or pandemic-era disruptions, those factors are really accelerants poured onto a fire that was already burning.

The reality is that the nation entered the pandemic with a severe housing shortage that had been accumulating for more than a decade.

When demand surged and borrowing costs fell during the pandemic, there was little available supply to absorb it. Prices climbed as families found themselves bidding against one another for an increasingly limited number of homes.

Now, as inflation and higher interest rates put additional pressure on the market, the shortage created after 2008 is becoming even more visible. It is perhaps best seen through the perspective of affordable housing providers. Unlike market-rate developers, affordable housing operators often have limited ability to raise rents to offset rising expenses, even though they are confronting many of the same economic pressures affecting the broader market.

According to the report, operating costs for affordable housing have increased dramatically in recent years, with insurance spiking more than 110 percent, and repairs and maintenance costs climbing 35 percent since 2017.

Meanwhile, multifamily housing starts have slowed, affordable housing shortages persist, and hundreds of thousands of existing affordable units are expected to see affordability restrictions expire in the years ahead.

These are serious challenges, and for years policymakers have debated housing affordability through the lens of monthly costs. They argue about mortgage rates, rent caps, insurance premiums, property taxes, zoning regulations, environmental reviews, institutional investors, and short-term economic trends. But the fact is, the country simply stopped building enough housing after 2008 and never made up the difference.

We must recognize that there is no way to fix this overnight, but there are solutions. First, we must start viewing housing as part of our essential economic infrastructure. A functioning economy depends on workers of all types — teachers, nurses, first responders — being able to afford to live near their jobs. Economic mobility depends on families having access to stable and affordable housing.

With that mindset, policymakers, investors, and housing organizations can then work together to strengthen the housing ecosystem, including by expanding access to capital, supporting nonprofit and emerging housing developers, preserving existing affordable housing stock, modernizing financing tools, and advancing federal, state, and local policies that encourage housing production and preservation.

The Great Recession officially ended in 2009, but the housing recession never did.

Until policymakers address the structural housing deficit that emerged from the financial crisis, Americans will continue to experience the consequences through higher rents, higher home prices, and fewer opportunities to achieve economic security.

Inflation may be today’s villain. But the story began long before inflation arrived.

Valerie White is head of National Housing Strategic Initiatives for Local Initiatives Support Corporation.
